clue.text: Macho director hosted by Hollywood Bowl?

parts.note: Hollywood is a district of Los Angeles, which crosswords shorten to the city's two initials.

indicators.note: A host takes a guest in and puts them up inside, so the letters either side close around whatever is being hosted.

parts.note: A bowl on the table is a dish.
On a film credit the director is the standing single letter D.

explanation.surface: A film director being wined and dined at a concert at the Hollywood Bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hollywood Bowl is one Los Angeles venue, which is what makes the two words look like a single name; the setter splits them and uses each half separately.
explanation.definitionFit: LADDISH means macho in the beer-and-banter sense, so the adjective swaps straight in for the clue's word.

clue.text: Wicked's Defying Gravity performed on stage

indicators.note: Whatever defies gravity is heading upwards, and upwards in a down entry means reading the letters back up the column.

parts.note: Wicked gives EVIL, which this down entry meets climbing back up.

explanation.surface: A song from the musical Wicked being belted out in the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: Defying Gravity is a song from Wicked, so the two italicised titles read as one theatre sentence and only the first of them is doing any work.
explanation.definitionFit: A LIVE show is one happening in front of you rather than recorded, which is what performing on stage means.

clue.text: Awful politician takes cocaine in a bunch of addresses

indicators.note: To take something is to let it inside you, so the surrounding letters open up and admit the piece named next.

parts.note: Something awful is dire.
A Tory is a member of the British Conservative party, one of the two politicians crosswords reach for.
C is the standing crossword abbreviation for cocaine.

explanation.surface: A grim MP caught taking drugs while giving a run of speeches.
explanation.walkthrough: The addresses of the definition are the postal kind, not the ones a politician delivers, and the surface leans on the wrong sense the whole way.
explanation.definitionFit: A DIRECTORY is the book that lists names beside their addresses, so it is a bunch of addresses bound together.

clue.text: Phrase Methuselah had (flipping pompous way of referring to himself)

parts.note: Methuselah is the setter, so the setter had is I'd

indicators.note: flipping means turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.words: pompous way of referring to himself
parts.note: moi, French for me, is an affected way of saying me

explanation.surface: The setter grumbles in an aside about his own habit of pompously calling himself 'moi'.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by their pseudonym, so Methuselah had becomes I'D. 'flipping' looks like a mild curse, but it reverses MOI.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is not obvious from its words, a turn of phrase.

clue.text: A B-52 possibly Spoonerised Love Shack?

definitions.note: the B-52 is a tall bouffant hairdo, after which the band was named

indicators.note: Spoonerised means given the treatment of the Reverend Spooner, who swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: care is love or affection, and it is said aloud with a hard K sound
a hut is a shack

explanation.surface: A nod to The B-52's, whose hit song was Love Shack, given a Spoonerism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'B-52' and 'Love Shack' point at the band and its hit, but the B-52 here is the beehive hairdo the band was named after. Say 'care hut', swap its opening sounds K and H, and you hear the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The B-52 is a beehive hairstyle, so it is one example of a style of cut and set hair.

clue.text: Our people getting into sea like jellyfish

indicators.note: Getting into something puts you bodily inside it, so this piece is planted between the letters either side.

parts.note: The Med is the everyday short name for the Mediterranean.
Like in the sense of in the manner of is as.
Our people are us, and the word goes in exactly as written.

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers wading into the sea and drifting about like jellyfish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sea like' looks as though it is finishing a simile; it is two unrelated scraps of wordplay with the swimmers dropped in between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A medusa is the free-swimming bell stage of a jellyfish, so the plural covers several of the creatures.

clue.text: Where to stop vessel twisting space and time

indicators.note: twisting means turning round, so the word for space is read backwards

parts.note: room means space, as in room to move
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A boat spins about, taking up space and time as it comes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Moorage is a place where boats are tied up, or the charge paid for berthing there.

clue.text: Aldi's reps freshened up spread

indicators.note: freshened up suggests a makeover, so these letters are given a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Sales representatives for the supermarket chain Aldi spruce up a buffet spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freshened up' rearranges the letters. Aldi is a German discount supermarket chain. 'spread' looks like a noun for a meal, but it is the past tense of the verb, distributed.
explanation.definitionFit: Dispersal is the act of scattering or distributing things widely, which is what spreading them does.

clue.text: Didn't take kindly to being hugged by solver, oddly

definitions.note: a past-tense verb phrase: to steal is to take, but not in a kindly way

indicators.note: being hugged by means held inside, so the short word goes within the picked letters
oddly takes the odd-numbered letters, first, third and fifth, of solver

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of solver

explanation.surface: Someone resents being hugged by a puzzle solver who behaves strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Didn't take kindly to' looks like one idiom for resenting; the definition stops before 'to', which is the word hugged by SLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Stole means took without permission, so it is taking done in a far from kindly way.

clue.text: Supported Davey rather than Miliband?

parts.note: Two politicians share the name, and Miliband had it in the public eye first, so pointing away from him says which of the pair is meant.
Ed Davey, leader of the Liberal Democrats, supplies his first name.

explanation.surface: Backing one party leader in preference to another.
explanation.walkthrough: Both men are Eds: Ed Miliband led Labour from 2010, Ed Davey the Liberal Democrats from 2020, so naming one instead of the other is really giving him a number.
explanation.definitionFit: To SECOND a motion is to back it formally, the committee-room sense of support.

clue.text: Overusing it could make you dizzy

indicators.note: could make you says these letters can be made into a new word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that overdoing something could leave you dizzy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could make you' signals that the letters of overusing it can be made into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Vertiginous describes vertigo, the whirling sensation of dizziness, or a height that would cause it.

clue.text: Tolkien creature has ring before Return of the King

parts.note: A ring drawn on the page is a circle, the letter O.

indicators.note: Before is positional: the piece named ahead of it is entered first, at the front.
A return is a coming back the way you came, so the letters named are written in the opposite order.

parts.note: Britain's king signs himself Charles Rex, CR, and that pair arrives here the other way about.

explanation.surface: A Tolkien monster laying hands on a ring before the last film of the trilogy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ring and The Return of the King are Tolkien's own titles, so the clue reads as a plot summary while both halves quietly do wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: ORCS are the goblin foot-soldiers Tolkien invented for Middle-earth, so the phrase names the species outright.

clue.text: Character opening seedy clubs let me see dirty film

indicators.note: The character that opens a word is its very first letter, and that letter alone is taken.

parts.note: Only the letter at the front of this word is wanted.
C is clubs on a bridge scoresheet, one of the four card suits crosswords lean on.
The noise a person makes while thinking is written um.

explanation.surface: A shady character breaking into a nightclub to watch a blue movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' wants to be a person in the film the surface is about; it means a letter, and the 'dirty film' at the end is the greasy layer on standing water.
explanation.definitionFit: SCUM is the filthy film that forms on the surface of a pond or a bath, a plain synonym once the film is not celluloid.

clue.text: Blender juiced each lemon

indicators.note: juiced means squeezed and pulped, so the letters are mashed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A kitchen appliance has squeezed every lemon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'juiced' rearranges each lemon. 'Blender' looks like the kitchen appliance; it is something that blends in with its background.
explanation.definitionFit: A chameleon changes colour to match its surroundings, so it blends in and is a natural camouflage expert.

clue.text: Flat deposit previously held in stock

definitions.meaning: The surface offers money put down on a rented flat; read plainly it is something flat that has been deposited on the ground.
A shop holds goods in stock, but stock is also livestock, and this was held inside the animal until the field received it.

explanation.surface: An estate agent's ledger: a deposit on an apartment that used to sit in shares.
explanation.walkthrough: Stock is the hinge: shares in the surface picture, cattle in the real one. There is no wordplay to unpick, only the one sense giving way to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the flat dropping a cow leaves in a field, matter that genuinely was held inside the stock beforehand.

clue.text: Lover of capers quietly orders starters for the entire restaurant

parts.note: P is piano in music, the mark telling a player to be quiet.
Orders in the sense of grades or classes are ranks.

indicators.note: A starter is what comes first, so each of the words after it gives up only the letter it opens with.

parts.note: Three words, each handing over the letter it begins with, in the order they are printed.

explanation.surface: A diner who loves capers quietly ordering first courses for everyone in the place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capers' does double duty in the picture: pickled flower buds on a restaurant menu, and escapades in the definition. 'Starters' plays the same trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A caper is a playful escapade, so the one who loves them is the person forever pulling them on other people.

clue.text: European on vacation mentioned charming private facilities

indicators.note: vacation means emptying, so European is emptied of its inner letters, keeping only its first and last

parts.note: only its outside letters are kept

indicators.note: mentioned means said aloud, so the word for charming is heard rather than read

parts.note: charming means sweet, which sounds like suite

explanation.surface: A European on holiday describes a hotel's private bathroom as charming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on vacation' empties European to EN; 'mentioned' turns SWEET into its sound-alike SUITE.
explanation.definitionFit: An en suite is a bathroom attached directly to a bedroom, a private washroom for that room's occupants.

clue.text: Good story moving leader more than words can say

indicators.note: moving leader says the first letter goes to the end of the word

parts.note: fine means good
a fable is a story, often with a moral

explanation.surface: A good story whose moving hero is beyond words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving leader' sends the F of FINE to the back, giving INEF. 'moving' looks like emotionally touching, but it is about shifting a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ineffable means too great or extreme to be expressed in words, so it is literally beyond description.

clue.text: Big gathering spread bad smell about base

parts.note: Jam is the spread you put on toast.
BO is body odour, the two initials standing for the smell.
Re means concerning, the about at the top of a memo.
e is the base of natural logarithms in mathematics.

explanation.surface: A bad smell being spread around the bottom of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread bad smell about' reads as one action, which is what disguises four separate scraps, and the base at the end is mathematical rather than architectural.
explanation.definitionFit: A JAMBOREE is a large celebratory rally, the word Scouting took for its international meetings.

clue.text: Crudely yawn and say "where was I?"

indicators.note: crudely means roughly, so these letters are roughly thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone yawns rudely and then asks where they had got to in the story.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the informal form of anyway, used to pick a conversation up after a digression, which is what 'where was I?' does.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyways is a colloquial filler for resuming a story after an interruption or tangent.

clue.text: Still seeing that heartless lie being swallowed

indicators.note: Swallowing takes a thing right inside, so this piece disappears into the middle of the word before it.

parts.note: Seeing that you are late and since you are late are the same conjunction.
The word for an untruth loses the I at its heart, leaving the letters that stood either side.

explanation.surface: Watching a small untruth get swallowed whole by the person told it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is the trap. It wants to be the adverb meaning even now, carrying the sentence on, and it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The still of the night is its SILENCE, the noun sense of still that survives mostly in that phrase.

clue.text: A little utensil Verdi used as top conductor

indicators.note: A little of something is a short run taken from inside it rather than the whole of it.

parts.note: The letters run on unbroken out of the end of one word and into the start of the next.

explanation.surface: A small piece of cutlery that Verdi once waved as a baton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' is the pivot: the surface wants Verdi on the podium, and the definition wants the metal that carries a current better than any other.
explanation.definitionFit: SILVER conducts electricity better than any other metal, so 'top' is a literal ranking rather than praise for a maestro.

clue.text: New team member communicating digitally

definitions.meaning: the recruit a club has just put under contract, in the sports-page sense
talking with the hands, digits having been fingers long before they were electronics

explanation.surface: A club's latest recruit tapping away at his phone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digitally' is the joke: not by phone or email but with the digits, the fingers, which is how sign language is done.
explanation.definitionFit: A club's new recruit is its latest signing, from the contract he signs; and signing is also holding a conversation in sign language.

clue.text: Cast member after being told this?

definitions.meaning: The surface wants an actor in the cast of a play; the other reading is a limb, a member, sitting in plaster.
'This' points at the answer itself, the thing said to a performer before curtain-up, which taken at its word lands them in that plaster.

explanation.surface: An actor in a company, and whatever it is somebody has just wished them.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to take apart here. The wish is theatre superstition, since saying good luck is held to invite the opposite, and the clue takes it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the traditional pre-show wish to an actor, and obeying it would put a member in a cast, which is how the clue reads both ways at once.

clue.text: Parliament embraces revolutionary way to contact MP?

indicators.note: A revolution turns a thing full circle, so the run of letters is met the other way about.
To embrace is to hold a thing within your arms, so the letters are sitting inside the word, unbroken.

parts.note: Five consecutive letters inside the word, read in the opposite order to the way they are printed.

explanation.surface: The Commons taking up a modern way of letting voters reach their members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a person, a firebrand loose in Parliament, and the clue comes close to describing itself, since the word Parliament really does contain what you write to one.
explanation.definitionFit: An EMAIL is one of several ways of writing to a member, so the question mark marks a definition by example.

clue.text: Vegan food fight's ending with saucer being thrown back

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the closing letter of the word fight; the possessive only links it to its ending

indicators.note: thrown back means turned round, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: a flying saucer is a UFO

explanation.surface: A food fight ends with a saucer being hurled back across a vegan table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saucer' looks like crockery being thrown; it is a flying saucer, a UFO, reversed to OFU after the T that ends 'fight'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tofu is bean curd made from soya, a staple protein in plant-based diets.

clue.text: Brief PM with wrong letter from EU? That's a bit of a shock

indicators.note: EU offers two letters; the wrong one, the U, is swapped for the other, the E

parts.note: Liz Truss was briefly the UK Prime Minister, in office for only 49 days in 2022

explanation.surface: A short-lived prime minister makes a gaffe over the European Union, which comes as a shock.
explanation.walkthrough: Liz Truss was Britain's shortest-serving prime minister. A 'shock' here is a mass of hair, not a surprise, and a tress is a lock of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A shock of hair is a thick mass of it, so a single lock or tress is a bit of a shock.

clue.text: Those turning heads with hot walks now and then

indicators.note: Now and then means at intervals rather than continuously, and the interval here is every other letter.

parts.note: Start at the second letter and take every other one straight through both words.

explanation.surface: Heads turning at the sight of somebody out walking in the heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' looks like an instruction to reverse something and is nothing of the sort; it belongs to the definition, where the turning is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: OWLS can swivel their heads about 270 degrees, so the phrase names them while also meaning attracting attention.

clue.text: One described by "river area"

indicators.note: In geometry a figure is described about another, drawn right round the outside of it, so the first piece ends up enclosed.

parts.note: R is the map abbreviation for river.
A is the standing abbreviation for area.
One as a Roman numeral is the single stroke I.

explanation.surface: A geography glossary entry that sums something up in just two words: river area.
explanation.walkthrough: A RIA is a drowned river valley open to the sea, so the quoted phrase is a straight definition as well as the source of the letters wrapped round the one.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a ria is a river's flooded lower valley, an arm of the sea, which the quoted phrase describes exactly.

clue.text: Joint liability established by court appearances?

parts.note: Appearing on court, in the sporting rather than the legal sense, means playing the racket game.
The joint wanted is the hinge halfway down your arm.

explanation.surface: A shared legal responsibility settled by turning up in court.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word points at the law — liability, established, court appearances — and none of it is legal; the court is the one with a net across the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A nagging injury that stops you playing properly is a liability in the everyday sense of a handicap, not the lawyer's sense the surface pushes.

clue.text: Increase in volume startled Al Green

indicators.note: startled means jolted, so the letters are jolted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; Al Green is an American soul singer

explanation.surface: The soul singer Al Green is startled when the volume is turned up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'startled' rearranges Al Green. 'in volume' looks like loudness to suit a singer; here it means size, bulk.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlarge something is to make it bigger, increasing its size or extent.

clue.text: John and the other three ultimately planning to dress up like colourful soldiers

indicators.note: Ultimately means at the very end, so each word gives up only the letter it finishes on.

parts.words: planning to dress up like colourful soldiers
parts.note: Seven words in a row, each contributing the letter it ends with, taken in the order they are printed.

explanation.surface: A group deciding to turn up dressed as brightly coloured soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John and the other three' pulls you towards the Beatles, and the costume in the surface is Sgt Pepper; the four actually meant are the evangelists.
explanation.definitionFit: John is one of the four GOSPELS, so he plus the remaining three name the set exactly.
